results.corrected_extracted: HHE 1: during a traffic stop and vehicle search, a police officer in a short-sleeved uniform and without gloves opened an unlabelled rubber container outside the vehicle, and a gust of wind blew powder from it onto the officer, who reported powder all over the officer and the uniform; the officer tried to brush it off and cleaned hands and arms with hand sanitizer. Within 5 minutes the officer was disoriented and lightheaded, with blurry vision. The ambulance arrived about 10 minutes after onset; EMS staff washed the exposed skin with water and found the officer alert, with blood pressure 175/127 mmHg, breathing rate 17 a minute, heart rate 105 a minute and pupils of 4 mm, reactive; during transport the officer reported intermittent trouble thinking and staying awake. At the emergency department, about 42 minutes after onset, the officer was alert with no constricted pupils; during transport and the visit the heart rate was 80–85, the breathing rate 15–21 and the blood pressure 149/77 to 159/104; the officer reported mild blurry vision there, which resolved after several hours; no laboratory tests were done; the discharge assessment was chemical exposure. The forensic laboratory identified fentanyl and methamphetamine in the powder left in the container (1.56 g), and fentanyl in a compressed tan powder (9.98 g); the Figure 1 legend says material in a paper wrapper beside the container contained fentanyl. Editors' notes: the one incident on file in which powder later found to contain fentanyl reached an officer's uncovered skin, as the account implies (short sleeves, no gloves, hands and arms cleaned, exposed skin washed); no sampling of the officer's skin or uniform is reported and no laboratory test was done, only vital signs and pupils being recorded; the powder also reached the uniform outdoors in wind, so breathing it in or contact with the eyes, nose or mouth are not excluded (the authors consider all routes possible, PDF p. 6); the powder also contained methamphetamine, and raised blood pressure and heart rate are among the effects of stimulants the authors list (PDF p. 5); constricted pupils or slowed breathing, signs of opioid toxicity, were not recorded.
results.note: Source has the officer attempting to brush the powder off and noting intermittent trouble thinking and staying awake (a self-report); vital signs and pupils were measured, so 'nothing was measured on the officer' is reworded. All numbers confirmed.

results.corrected_extracted: HHE 2: four officers developed symptoms while responding to a 911 call about an unconscious person with a possible overdose in a hotel room. Three entered, saw drug paraphernalia and powders scattered in plain view and heard the toilet flushed many times; they wore short sleeves, two wore gloves on entry and the third put gloves on shortly after, and they took turns to put on half-facepiece respirators with P-100 filters once powders were seen. One went back to headquarters to process a search warrant, using a computer and a camera used in the room; the fourth officer, who did not enter the room, helped there, handling the camera and other items from the room that had no visible contamination, and (Table 1) also cleaned gear and a vehicle at headquarters. Symptoms (lightheadedness or dizziness in all, with blurry vision, weakness, warmth, sweating, headache, numbness of both hands and the tongue, or feeling drunk, high or groggy) began about 25 to 90 minutes after the initial response for the three who entered, and about 30–45 minutes after first handling the equipment for the fourth (Table 1). One officer at the scene was helped out of the room, slumped against the wall and then to the ground, and improved rapidly after a colleague gave one dose of intranasal naloxone. Before transport all four were decontaminated (clothing and equipment removed, showered or washed with water, fresh clothing). None was reported to have depressed breathing; in the emergency department all had normal temperatures and were alert and oriented, none had documented constricted pupils, and the electrocardiograms were normal; blood pressure and heart rate were normal to raised, three had normal to raised breathing rates, and the fourth officer a rate ranging from 9 to 20 a minute; the officer given naloxone had no blood test, and the urine of all four was negative on a screen for cannabinoids, phencyclidine, cocaine, opiates, amphetamines, benzodiazepines and barbiturates; all were discharged after several hours. The emergency physicians' impressions were possible accidental overdose for the officer given naloxone and possible fentanyl exposure for the other three (Table 1). In the hotel room the laboratory identified dibutylone, N-ethylpentylone (2.87 g), heroin (0.14 g), para-fluoroisobutyryl fentanyl, cocaine, methamphetamine and fentanyl (0.14 g) (Table 2); the Results call these opioids, cocaine, methamphetamine and cathinones. Editors' notes: the opiate screen cannot detect fentanyl or its analogues, and most amphetamine screens do not readily detect synthetic cathinones (the article, PDF p. 7), so no officer had a test able to detect the fentanyl or the analogue found in the room, and whether the amphetamine screen used could detect the cathinones is not stated; when the urine was collected is not reported; no sampling of the air, of surfaces or of the officers' skin or clothing is reported.
results.note: Added from Table 1: the fourth officer also cleaned gear and a vehicle. Source does not tie no depressed breathing to after decontamination. Cathinone detection is hedged in the source (most screens), so the editors' conclusion is hedged. Numbers confirmed.

results.corrected_extracted: The authors judge that the five officers' health effects were not consistent with severe (life-threatening or late-stage) opioid toxicity, whose signs include profound lethargy, shallow, slow or absent breathing, constricted pupils, slow heart rate and low body temperature; they write that low-dose opioid exposure may give milder symptoms along a continuum, that non-specific symptoms such as nausea and lightheadedness reported by the officers fit it, and that the improvement after naloxone in one officer suggests that opioids were a substantial component of a mixed exposure; low-level exposure to opioids combined with other drugs, particularly stimulants, might be consistent with the variety of effects, and adulterants or contaminants in illicit drugs might also lead to a variety of effects. The authors add that perceived risk might contribute to the observed effects: it has been associated with anxiety and symptom reporting apart from physical exposure, and its relationships with the exposures and the officers' clinical status were not assessed. Breathing in, absorption through mucous membranes, swallowing and absorption through the skin were all possible routes in both incidents; brief skin contact with fentanyl powder, or powder of an analogue, is not expected to cause toxic effects if visible contamination is promptly removed (citing three sources, among them the ACMT and AACT statement); alcohol-based hand sanitizer, as used in HHE 1, may increase absorption of fentanyl powder. Negative urine screens do not rule out exposure: opiate screens will not detect synthetic opioids such as fentanyl, synthetic cathinones are not readily detected by most amphetamine screens, the amphetamine and cocaine screens were negative at cut-offs of 500 ng/mL and 150 ng/mL, and results under a cut-off are reported as negative. Stated limitations: retrospective evaluations, interviews weeks to months after the incidents, review of the acute emergency department records only, so medical conditions not evaluated at the time could not be assessed afterwards, and toxicological data not always available. Editors' notes: nausea appears in no officer's reported symptoms in the Results or Table 1 (PDF pp. 3–4, 15); the reading of the naloxone response rests on one uncontrolled observation in an officer who had no blood test and whose urine screen could not detect fentanyl; no exposure was measured (no sampling of air, surfaces or skin) and no officer had a test able to detect fentanyl, so the article neither confirms nor excludes opioid poisoning in any officer.
results.note: Source says stimulant mixtures might be consistent with (not explain) the effects, and adulterants might lead to effects generally. Added: authors suggest perceived risk might contribute; limitation that unevaluated medical conditions could not be assessed. Editors' note reworded.

All parts checked, including NIOSH report 2018-0118-3331 (Jackson, Chiu, Hornsby-Myers; November 2018; two officers, locked metal box, no fentanyl or other opioid identified) and Chiu's reference list, which does not cite it.

key_findings.correction: HHE 1: during a traffic stop and vehicle search, an officer in a short-sleeved uniform and without gloves opened an unlabelled rubber container outside the vehicle, and a gust of wind blew powder from it onto the officer, who reported that it was all over the officer and the uniform; the officer tried to brush it off and cleaned hands and arms with hand sanitizer. Within 5 minutes the officer was disoriented and lightheaded, with blurry vision. The ambulance arrived about 10 minutes after onset; EMS staff washed the exposed skin with water and found the officer alert, with blood pressure 175/127 mmHg, breathing rate 17 a minute, heart rate 105 a minute and pupils of 4 mm, reactive; during transport the officer reported intermittent trouble thinking and staying awake.
key_findings.note: Source: the officer attempted to brush the powder off, reported the powder all over officer and uniform, and noted the trouble thinking and staying awake (PDF p. 3).
Minor: the source has the person observed by the officers to be intoxicated (PDF p. 4).

key_findings.correction: Before transport all four HHE 2 officers were decontaminated (clothing and equipment removed, showered or washed with water, fresh clothing). None was reported to have depressed breathing. In the emergency department all had normal temperatures and normal to raised blood pressure and heart rate; three had normal to raised breathing rates, and the fourth (the officer who never entered the room) a breathing rate ranging from 9 to 20 a minute; all were alert and oriented, none had documented constricted pupils, and the electrocardiograms showed no abnormality. Three had blood tests that ruled out conditions including volume depletion and low blood sugar; the officer given naloxone had no blood test. The urine of all four was negative on a screen for cannabinoids, phencyclidine, cocaine, opiates, amphetamines, benzodiazepines and barbiturates. All four were discharged after several hours of observation, with their symptoms improved.
key_findings.note: The officer who returned to headquarters (LEO 3) also handled items there, so 'the officer who handled items at headquarters' does not identify the officer with the 9 to 20 rate (LEO 5).

key_findings.correction: The authors judge that the officers' health effects were not consistent with severe (life-threatening or late-stage) opioid toxicity, whose signs include profound lethargy, shallow, slow or absent breathing, constricted pupils, slow heart rate and low body temperature. They write that low-dose opioid exposure may give milder symptoms along a continuum, that non-specific symptoms such as nausea and lightheadedness reported by the officers fit that continuum, and that the improvement of the officer given naloxone suggests opioids were a substantial component of the mixed exposure; low-level exposure to opioids combined with other drugs, particularly stimulants, might be consistent with the variety of effects, and adulterants or contaminants in illicit drugs might also lead to a variety of effects.
key_findings.note: Source: might be consistent with, not might explain; the adulterant sentence concerns exposed individuals in general (PDF p. 5).
The paragraph opens by saying perceived risk might contribute to the observed effects (PDF p. 6); worth adding.

key_findings.correction: Conclusions and prevention: multiple drugs, including opioids such as fentanyl and stimulants such as cocaine or methamphetamine, were present at each incident; the effects were not consistent with severe, life-threatening opioid toxicity but needed medical attention and kept the officers from their duties; the authors write that the potential for risk is clear from these investigations, that assuming both that the effects merely reflect perceived risk and that no protective measures are needed endangers responders and the people they help, and that prevention (controls, protective equipment, training on actual against perceived risk) should start now; they call for surveillance, laboratory simulations, guidelines for medical evaluation and timely prospective toxicological testing, noting that serum fentanyl peaks within minutes of an intravenous or transmucosal dose and that urine detection windows vary.
key_findings.note: The warning is about the joint assumption (perception only, and no protective measures needed), not about attributing effects to perceived risk alone (PDF p. 8).

reporting_issues.correction: issue: One HHE 2 officer, the one who handled items at headquarters and never entered the room, had an emergency department breathing rate ranging from 9 to 20 a minute, whose lower end is below the normal resting range the article gives for the HHE 1 officer (12 to 15 a minute), yet the article states that none of the four was reported to have depressed breathing and does not discuss the low reading or when it was taken. | consequence: What the reading of 9 reflected cannot be told from the article; the statement that no officer had depressed breathing rests on what was reported, not on this value.

issue: The ACMT and AACT position statement is cited (reference 30) as published in Clinical Toxicology in 2017, volume 56, pages 391–400. Editors' note: the copy on file is the Journal of Medical Toxicology version (13(4):347–351), which Persaud and Jennings (2020) and Herman et al. (2020) also cite; the NIOSH report on file (Jackson et al., 2018, PDF p. 22, printed D-2) cites a Clinical Toxicology version at 56(4):297–300. | consequence: None for the findings; the PDFs on file point to a second publication in Clinical Toxicology, but at other pages than reference 30 gives, so its pages look like a citation error.

risk_of_bias.note: Design case-series and overall high for any causal conclusion: agree. Instrument: METHODS §5.3 assigns no instrument to case series (the card states the design's limits); the round-brief rule the card cites for JBI prevalence is not in docs/STUDY-CARD-BRIEF.md or this round's BRIEF-companion.md, so the editor should confirm it. Domain 7 'partial-yes' is generous (testing differed by officer and none could detect fentanyl); 'no' fits, without changing the overall.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial rather than minor. The title presents the health effects as caused by opioid exposure and the abstract states that the officers were exposed to opioid and stimulant drugs, which nothing measured shows; with the naloxone inference, the misattributed nausea and the statement that the potential for risk is clear from these investigations, the framing outruns the data. 'claimed' does not mention the title (PDF p. 1).

missed: Title (PDF p. 1): Health Effects from Unintentional Occupational Exposure to Opioids among Law Enforcement Officers presents causation the data cannot show; it belongs in interpretation_gap.claimed.

Prevention for First Responders (PDF pp. 8–9): the authors write that understanding that incidental skin contact with suspected fentanyl powder can be remedied by washing with soap and water may make acute anxiety less likely than believing any skin contact will cause a life-threatening overdose; relevant to both answers.

cannot_establish and risk-of-bias domain 6 say no officer had a test able to detect synthetic cathinones; the source says only that most amphetamine screens do not readily detect them and does not name the assay used (PDF p. 7).

design_detail says nothing was sampled on surfaces and cannot_establish that nothing was measured on the officers: residues were collected as evidence (Table 2) and vital signs were measured; better 'no exposure sampling (air, surface wipes, skin) and no exposure biomarker'.
exposure.measurement says the officer brushed the powder off; the source says the officer attempted to (PDF p. 3).

Timeline (Jackson et al., 2018): the card ties non-citation to web references accessed in October 2018, but references 52 and 53 are dated 2 January 2019 and 14 November 2018 (PDF p. 13), so the article was still revised after that November 2018 report; and references 8 and 9 were accessed in March and September 2018.
Checked and accurate: the timeline entry on Herman et al. (2020), against Herman p. 112 and reference 9 (p. 114).
